title: Addition vs Multiplication
coreInsight: Disjoint alternatives combine by addition, while sequential choices combine by multiplication when each branch's continuations are counted correctly.
narrativeTransition: List a small outfit-style choice space, rearrange it into a grid, and let the rectangular structure reveal multiplication; contrast it with genuinely separate alternatives.
commonMisconceptions: The words 'or' and 'and' mechanically determine addition or multiplication in every problem.
Every branch is assumed to have the same number of continuations.
Overlapping alternatives can be added without correction.
Counting steps and counting final outcomes are the same thing.

title: Systematic Listing & Trees
coreInsight: Organization turns an informal list of possibilities into a structure that can be checked for completeness and duplication.
narrativeTransition: Choose a problem whose branches are not uniform enough for one multiplication, forcing the learner to organize outcomes explicitly.
commonMisconceptions: Any list is systematic if it is long enough.
Duplicate outcomes are harmless.
Seeing a pattern early means the list can stop.
A path of decisions and the final outcome are always identical objects.

title: Factorials & Ordered Arrangements
coreInsight: When distinct objects fill ordered positions, the number of available choices shrinks one position at a time, creating factorial products.
narrativeTransition: Fill a row of positions with distinct people and display the shrinking choice count before naming factorial notation.
commonMisconceptions: Factorial applies whenever objects are selected, even if order is irrelevant.
0! should equal 0.
Repeated or identical objects can be treated as fully distinct without consequence.
Two arrangements with different order can represent the same outcome when the problem ignores order.

title: Casework
coreInsight: A difficult universe can be partitioned into cases that are exhaustive, non-overlapping, and easier to count.
narrativeTransition: After systematic listing, ask the learner how they can prove that every possibility has been captured, then sort outcomes by a structural feature.
commonMisconceptions: Cases may overlap without adjustment.
A few natural cases are automatically exhaustive.
Cases are useful even when each is as difficult as the original problem.
The best case split need not reflect the problem's actual constraint.

title: Complementary Counting
coreInsight: When the desired set is awkward but its opposite is simple, count the complete universe and remove the complement.
narrativeTransition: Modify a clean casework problem such as 'exactly one zero' into an 'at least one' version so the old cases overlap and the complement becomes dramatically simpler.
commonMisconceptions: The complement is just one undesirable case rather than every outcome outside the event.
The subtraction universe can be chosen arbitrarily.
At least one and exactly one are interchangeable.
Complementary counting always requires probability notation.

title: Overcounting & Symmetry
coreInsight: One mathematical outcome may have several descriptions or orderings; when every true outcome is represented the same number of times, divide by that multiplicity.
narrativeTransition: Count an unordered selection as though it were an ordered lineup, then group the duplicate descriptions that actually represent the same object.
commonMisconceptions: Overcounting can always be fixed by dividing by 2.
Every outcome is automatically overcounted equally often.
Different descriptions necessarily represent different mathematical outcomes.
Symmetry can be invoked without checking that the multiplicity is uniform.

title: Choosing Without Order
coreInsight: Combinations arise by counting ordered selections and then removing the artificial order that does not matter to the outcome.
narrativeTransition: Show how many ordered lineups correspond to the same committee, then divide away the order before introducing combination notation.
commonMisconceptions: Permutation-versus-combination problems can be solved by keyword matching.
It is unnecessary to define what counts as the same outcome.
n choose r is a formula with no relation to ordered counting.
Dividing by r! is arbitrary.

title: Sets, Intersections & Venn Diagrams
coreInsight: Sets represent membership in conditions, and intersections make simultaneous membership and overlap explicit.
narrativeTransition: Sort objects satisfying two properties into visible regions so the overlap becomes a mathematical object instead of a bookkeeping accident.
commonMisconceptions: Union and intersection are reversed.
Mathematical 'or' must be exclusive.
Everything belongs to at least one displayed set.
The region outside both sets can be ignored when it is part of the universe.

title: Inclusion–Exclusion
coreInsight: Adding overlapping groups counts their intersection multiple times, so the repeated contribution must be corrected.
narrativeTransition: Color two sets and then add their counts so the intersection visibly receives two layers; remove the extra layer rather than introducing the formula first.
commonMisconceptions: The overlap should always be subtracted, even for disjoint sets.
Higher-order overlaps in three-set problems can be ignored.
The inclusion–exclusion signs should be memorized without tracking multiplicity.
Union size equals the sum of set sizes whenever the sets look mostly separate.

title: Grid Paths & Pascal's Triangle
coreInsight: Path counts can be built recursively from predecessor states, and unrestricted shortest paths correspond to choosing which step positions have each direction.
narrativeTransition: Fill a small grid by adding counts from predecessor cells, then reinterpret one path as a choice of step positions to connect the recursion to combinations.
commonMisconceptions: Counting grid points is the same as counting paths.
A combination formula still works unchanged when obstacles alter the path structure.
Recursive and choose-based solutions count different things.
Every path problem requires explicitly listing routes.

title: Probability as Counting
coreInsight: Probability measures an event relative to a complete probability model; for equally likely discrete outcomes, it is the fraction of the sample space that is favorable.
narrativeTransition: Reuse an outcome tree the learner already understands, then color successful leaves and compare them with the entire set of equally likely leaves.
commonMisconceptions: All outcomes that are easy to list are equally likely.
The sample space can be incomplete.
Probability is just the number of favorable outcomes.
The numerator and denominator may refer to different universes.

title: Dependent Events
coreInsight: After one event occurs, the state and therefore later probabilities may change.
narrativeTransition: Remove an object without replacement and let the denominator physically shrink before asking for the next probability.
commonMisconceptions: Original probabilities can be multiplied unchanged after the state changes.
Independent and mutually exclusive mean the same thing.
Replacement has no effect on dependence.
Conditioning on what happened can be ignored.

title: Complementary Probability
coreInsight: Probability inherits complementary counting: an event and its complement exhaust the sample space, so their probabilities add to 1.
narrativeTransition: Present an 'at least one' probability problem and explicitly invite the learner to recognize the complementary-counting strategy they already know.
commonMisconceptions: Subtracting one bad outcome is the same as subtracting the full complement.
Not exactly one means none.
An event and the proposed complement may fail to exhaust the sample space.
The complement rule is unrelated to earlier counting ideas.
